calls.title: Custom LLM Experiment Overview
calls.text: {"summary": "This experiment involved training a tiny word-level language model, Karpathy's nanoGPT, on two different corpora. The experiments compared training on a starter corpus alone versus the starter corpus augmented with custom teaching files.", "details": [{"text": "The model used Karpathy's nanoGPT, which has 2 blocks, 4 heads, 64-number embeddings, and a 48-token context.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Experiment 1 used the starter corpus, while Experiment 2 used the starter corpus plus three plain-text teaching files.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The training steps for both experiments were set to 3,000, which was deemed enough practice for the small model.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "The learning rate was set to 0.001, which was large enough for progress within 3,000 steps but small enough to avoid overshooting.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "The vocabulary for Experiment 1 was 136, while Experiment 2 had a vocabulary of 481.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "The fixed settings across both experiments included the seed 42, model size, batch size, steps, learning rate, and the 48-case eval suite.", "section": "S4"}]}

calls.title: Evidence Samples and Loss
calls.text: {"summary": "Evidence samples and loss relate to a Custom LLM Experiment involving samples and loss measurements. The experiment involved tracking changes in samples and loss values across different steps and experiments.", "details": [{"text": "Samples are recorded for Experiment 1 and Experiment 2, with different content at different steps.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Step-0 samples were described as 'word soup'.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "By step 1,500, samples transitioned from random words to complete template sentences.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "In Experiment 1, all 8 halfway and final sentences existed word for word in the corpus, and 2 were validation passages the model never trained on.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Loss values are measured for fixed panels consisting of 20 training and 20 validation passages.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Experiment 1 starter loss at Step 0 was 4.926 for training and 4.928 for validation.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Experiment 2 expanded loss at Step 0 was 6.187 for training and 6.167 for validation.", "section": "S1"}]}

calls.title: RAG and LLM Limitations
calls.text: {"summary": "RAG and LLM limitations involve issues such as incorrect information generation and the inability to fully prevent errors. LLMs can generate misinformation even when using factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context.", "details": [{"text": "LLMs can provide incorrect information.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "When Google first demonstrated its LLM tool \"Bard\" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "MIT Technology Review gave the example of an AI-generated response stating, \"The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama.\"", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title \"Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?\" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The LLM did not \"know\" or \"understand\" the context of the title, generating a false statement.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "This technique has been called \"prompt stuffing.\"", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.", "section": "S1"}]}

calls.title: RAG Process Flow
calls.text: {"summary": "Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to access and utilize data beyond their original training set. This process involves converting data into embeddings, storing them in a vector database, and using a retriever to select relevant documents to augment the query before the LLM synthesizes an answer.", "details": [{"text": "Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.", "section": "S2"}]}

calls.title: RAG Challenges
calls.text: {"summary": "RAG presents several challenges that do not eliminate all issues with large language models. These challenges include the possibility of hallucinations, limitations in recognizing insufficient information, and issues related to RAG poisoning.", "details": [{"text": "RAG does not prevent hallucinations in LLMs because the LLM can still hallucinate around the source material in its response.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "While RAG improves the accuracy of large language models (LLMs), it does not eliminate all challenges.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "One limitation is that while RAG reduces the need for frequent model retraining, it does not remove it entirely.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Without specific training, models may generate answers even when they should indicate uncertainty, which can arise when the model lacks the ability to assess its own knowledge limitations.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "An LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "When faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "These issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Clock Tower X used RAG poisoning to flood the information space with sites and content sympathetic to Israel.", "section": "S2"}]}

calls.title: Transformer Architecture
calls.text: {"summary": "The Transformer is a family of artificial neural network architectures based on the multi-head attention mechanism. It converts input data like text, images, or audio into a sequence of numerical representations called tokens. Transformers can be parallelized across sequence positions during training, unlike recurrent neural networks.", "details": [{"text": "In deep learning, the transformer is a family of artificial neural network architectures based on the multi-head attention mechanism.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Input data such as text, images, or audio is converted to a sequence of numerical representations called tokens, and each token is converted into a vector through an embedding layer.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "At each layer, each token is then contextualized within the scope of the context window with other (unmasked) tokens via a parallel multi-head attention mechanism, allowing the signal for key tokens to be amplified and less important tokens to be diminished.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Because self-attention alone is permutation-invariant, transformers inject positional information, typically through positional encodings or learned positional embeddings, so token order can affect the output.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "All transformers have the same primary components: Tokenizers, which convert text into tokens.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "All transformers have the same primary components: Embedding layer, which converts tokens and positions of the tokens into vector representations.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "All transformers have the same primary components: Transformer layers, which carry out repeated transformations on the vector representations, extracting more and more linguistic information. These consist of alternating attention and feedforward layers.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "All transformers have the same primary components: Un-embedding layer, which converts the final vector representations back to a probability distribution over the tokens.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Each integer token identifier is converted into an embedding vector via a lookup table. Equivalently stated, it multiplies a one-hot representation of the token identifier by an embedding matrix $M$.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "The dimension of an embedding vector is called hidden size or embedding size and written as $d_{\text{emb}}$ or $d_{\text{model}}$.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "A positional encoding is a fixed-size vector representation of the relative positions of tokens within a sequence: it provides the transformer model with information about where the words are in the input sequence.", "section": "S6"}]}

calls.title: Transformer Training Methods
calls.text: {"summary": "Transformer training methods cover techniques for stabilizing training, regularization, pretraining and fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, and various language modeling tasks. These methods address issues like convergence, overfitting, and model size.", "details": [{"text": "The plain transformer architecture had difficulty in converging, and the authors recommended using learning rate warmup, where the learning rate linearly scales up from 0 to a maximal value for the first part of training before decaying again.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Using layer normalization before multihead attention and feedforward layers instead of after has been found to stabilize training, leading to the \"pre-LN Transformer,\" which is more commonly used than the original \"post-LN Transformer.\"", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The original transformer used dropout during training to reduce overfitting, applying it to the output of each sublayer before its residual connection and to the sums of token embeddings and positional encodings.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The original paper also used label smoothing, which replaces a certain target distribution with one that assigns a small amount of probability to alternative tokens, to improve generalization by going against overconfidence in the training targets.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Transformers are typically first pretrained by self-supervised learning on a large generic dataset, followed by supervised fine-tuning on a small task-specific dataset.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "Tasks for pretraining and fine-tuning commonly include language modeling, next-sentence prediction, question answering, reading comprehension, sentiment analysis, and paraphrasing.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "Knowledge distillation is a method for training a smaller model, called a \"student,\" to reproduce the output behavior of a larger \"teacher\" model using the teacher's output probability distribution, intermediate representations, or attention patterns.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "Language modeling tasks include \"masked,\" \"autoregressive,\" and \"prefixLM\" classes.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "In a masked task, one or more tokens are masked out, and the model produces a probability distribution predicting what the masked-out tokens are based on the context, with the loss function typically being the sum of log-perplexities for the masked-out tokens.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "In an autoregressive task, the entire sequence is masked at first, and the model predicts the first token, and then subsequent tokens are predicted sequentially.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "In a prefixLM task, the sequence is divided into two parts, where the model predicts the first token of the second part, and then subsequent tokens are predicted sequentially.", "section": "S5"}]}

calls.title: Transformer Efficient Implementations
calls.text: {"summary": "Transformer Efficient Implementations cover various techniques to make transformer models more efficient for inference and training. These methods include optimizations for KV caching, continuous batching, quantization, FlashAttention, Multi-Query Attention, speculative decoding, and sub-quadratic attention graphs.", "details": [{"text": "The transformer model has been implemented in standard deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The KV caching method saves the computed key and value vectors at each attention block, so that they are not recomputed at each new token.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "PagedAttention applies memory paging to KV caching.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Continuous batching adds new requests to batch and removes completed requests between decoding iterations instead of waiting for every request in a batch to finish.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "Quantization can reduce memory use and data transfer costs and can improve inference speed on hardware that supports low precision arithmetic.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "FlashAttention is an algorithm that implements the transformer attention mechanism efficiently on a GPU.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "FlashAttention-2 offers enhancements in work partitioning and parallelism, enabling it to achieve up to 230 TFLOPs/s on A100 GPUs (FP16/BF16), a 2x speed increase over the original FlashAttention.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "Multi-Query Attention changes the Multihead Attention mechanism by having just one $W^{K},W^{V}$, which increases inference speed.", "section": "S6"}, {"text": "Speculative decoding is a method to accelerate token decoding by quickly computing future tokens and then verifying them.", "section": "S7"}, {"text": "Random Feature Attention can be computed in linear time, as we can compute the matrix $\\varphi (k_{i})v_{i}^{T}$", "section": "S10"}]}
